question.value: What are the gas mass-loss rates and wind velocities of red supergiants in the open cluster RSGC1 from ALMA CO(2-1) observations, and what new mass-loss rate prescription can be derived for red supergiants?

evidence.quote: We aim to derive a new mass-loss rate prescription for RSGs that is not afflicted with some uncertainties inherent in preceding studies.
With this study, we aim to provide the first measurements of the gas mass-loss rates (M˙ CO) of RSGs as a function of the specific RSG age.
The 14 RSGs (F01–F14) and 1 post-RSG (F15) in RSGC1 (see Table 2 in Davies et al. 2008) were observed with ALMA on 2015 June 9 and 11 for proposal code 2013.1.01200.S.
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA2013.1.01200.S.
We requested observations at both band 9, centred on the CO v=0 J=6-5 rotational line transition and band 6, centred on the CO v=0 J=2-1 rotational line transition, but only the latter were obtained.

findings_qualitative.value: CO-derived gas mass-loss rates for F01, F02, and F03 are systematically lower by a factor of ~2 than previous SED-derived values primarily because their measured terminal wind velocities (8-15 km/s) are lower than the 25 km/s assumed in SED studies.

findings_qualitative.value: F01, F02, F03, and F04 have mass-loss rates below the nuclear burning rate (core-He burning dominated evolution), whereas F13 has an order-of-magnitude higher mass-loss rate (42 x 10^-6 Msun/yr) where wind mass loss dominates evolution.

findings_qualitative.value: Quiescent RSG mass loss following the new CO-calibrated prescription is insufficient to strip the H-rich envelope of a single 25 Msun star, meaning such stars will explode as RSGs (Type II SNe) rather than evolving to Wolf-Rayet stars.

evidence.quote: A reduction of the RSG mass-loss rate implies that quiescent RSG mass loss is not enough to strip a single star’s hydrogen-rich envelope. Upon core collapse such single stars would explode as RSGs.

claims.hypothesis: Gas mass-loss rates of coeval red supergiants in RSGC1 can be measured directly from ALMA CO(2-1) line profiles without the uncertain wind velocity and dust-to-gas ratio assumptions inherent in SED dust modelling.
claims.experiment: Observe 14 RSGs and 1 post-RSG in RSGC1 with ALMA in Band 6 CO(2-1) and model the spatially/spectrally resolved line profiles of the 5 detected RSGs with the non-LTE radiative transfer code GASTRoNOoM.
claims.result: For F01, F02, F03, and F04, terminal wind velocities are 8–15 km/s and Mdot_CO values are 1.8–4.0 x 10^-6 Msun/yr, systematically lower by a factor of ~2 than Mdot_SED from Beasor et al. (2020); once corrected for the measured terminal velocities, Mdot_CO and Mdot_SED agree within ~32% (average factor ~0.9), implying a gas-to-dust ratio of 235 ± 71.
claims.finding: CO(2-1) observations directly constrain the lower expansion velocities of RSG winds in RSGC1, showing that quiescent RSG mass-loss rates are lower than previously inferred from dust SEDs.

evidence.quote: The CO gas mass-loss rate values of those red supergiants in common with Beasor et al. (2020) are systematically lower, on average by a factor of ∼2 (see Table 1) — although we here must provide the caveat of dealing with small number statistics.

Correcting for the terminal velocities as deduced from the ALMA CO(2-1) data, M˙ CO and M˙ SED agree very well for the three sources in common to both studies (F01, F02, and F03) with average difference being a factor ∼0.9 and maximum percentage difference of 32% (see also last two columns in Table 1).

claims.hypothesis: A combined empirical mass-loss rate prescription dependent on bolometric luminosity and initial mass can accurately predict quiescent Mdot_CO for M-type red supergiants with Teff between ~3200 and 3800 K.
claims.experiment: Jointly fit Mdot_SED measurements from four open clusters and Mdot_CO measurements from RSGC1 using multivariate least squares and Monte Carlo error estimation (Eq. 8), then test predictions against multi-line JCMT CO observations of Galactic RSGs (alpha Ori, mu Cep, VX Sgr, VY CMa).
claims.result: Eq. (8) yields b = 3.50 (+0.60/-0.46), S = -1.68 (+0.31/-0.40), R_SED = 1.77 (+0.58/-0.46), and Delta_R = 0.49 (+0.44/-0.41), and reproduces the CO mass-loss rates of alpha Ori, mu Cep, and VX Sgr with an average difference of ~30%, while underpredicting the extreme RSGs F13 and VY CMa by factors of ~10 and ~6.6.
claims.finding: The new mass-loss prescription accurately predicts quiescent mass-loss rates for M-type RSGs (3200–3800 K), whereas extreme RSGs like F13 and VY CMa experience a different, stronger mass-loss mode.

evidence.quote: The analysis presented in App. G proves that Eq. (8) predicts the gas mass-loss rate for M-type red supergiants with effective temperature between ∼3200 – 3800 K with good accuracy, the average difference only being ∼30% (see Table G.1).

Both F13 and VY CMa are indicative of a stronger, potentially eruptive, mass-loss process that breaks from the prescription given in Eq. (8); they demonstrate that one should be careful about applying any M˙ -prescription, including Eq. (8), more globally in stellar evolution models as they will not reproduce the behaviour of those extreme RSGs; see also the recent discussion by Massey et al. (2022).

claims.hypothesis: Red supergiants undergo a phase change during their evolution from a nuclear-burning-dominated quiescent wind phase to a wind-dominated intense mass-loss phase, but this is still insufficient to strip the entire H-rich envelope of single ~25 Msun stars in RSGC1.
claims.experiment: Compare Mdot_CO against nuclear burning rates, evolve a 25 Msun star to core carbon depletion in MESA using Eq. (8), and compare the required lifetime fraction in the strong mass-loss phase with Bayesian binomial statistics (1 out of 14 RSGs in RSGC1).
claims.result: In MESA, Eq. (8) removes only 1.93 Msun out of 11.97 Msun of the H-rich envelope (requiring 6.20x higher mass loss to strip the envelope, or F = 55% of the RSG lifetime at F13's 10.43x enhanced rate), whereas binomial statistics give F = 10.9 (+17/-8.5)% (90% credible interval).
claims.finding: Single ~25 Msun stars in RSGC1 will not strip their entire H-rich envelopes via quiescent or F13-like enhanced RSG winds and will explode as RSGs (Type II SNe) upon core collapse unless much stronger (>~10^-4 Msun/yr) dynamical ejections occur.

evidence.quote: Using the new prescription of Eq. (8), only 1.93 M⊙ of the hydrogen-rich stellar envelope is lost (out of a total envelope mass of 11.97 M⊙) implying that such massive stars would explode as RSG upon core-collapse (see Fig. 5).

This tension between the outcome of number statistics and the fraction of time needed to strip the H-envelope during the RSG phase when considering both the quiescent and (potentially eruptive) high mass-loss rate phase induces the suggestion that the RSGs in RSGC1 will not be able to strip their entire H-envelope and will explode as RSG upon core-collapse.

referee_caveats_inferred: Only 4 stars (F01-F04) in a single cluster (RSGC1) have CO detections used in the regression fit (Eq. 8), and all 4 lie in a narrow luminosity range (log L/Lsun = 5.24-5.56) at the top of the mass-loss distribution while 10 other cluster members are non-detections.

Consequently, the luminosity slope (b = 3.50) and initial mass dependence (S = -1.68) of the new prescription are entirely driven by the literature dust-SED measurements from Beasor et al., with the ALMA CO data only providing a constant zero-point offset (Delta_R = 0.49 ± 0.43) that is barely a ~1.1-sigma shift.
